vo: The Sony executives stood tall, smiling under the flashing cameras.

vc: A secret corporate document stamped 'NINTENDO & PHILIPS AGREEMENT' resting on a transatlantic flight tray table beside an airplane window overlooking European clouds
vo: Behind Sony's back, Nintendo had flown executives to Europe and signed an exclusive partnership with Sony’s bitter arch-rival, Philips.

label: PARALYZED DISBELIEF
vc: A row of Sony executives sitting in the convention audience, frozen completely still with wide, unblinking eyes, mouths slightly agape in utter shock
vo: Sony executives in the audience sat in paralyzed disbelief.

label: FACES DRAINED

vo: Their faces drained of color.

label: HONOR-BOUND CODE
vc: A traditional Japanese samurai katana sword resting on a formal lacquered wooden stand, with a snapped corporate seal lying in front of it
vo: In the rigid, honor-bound culture of Japanese corporate business, this was not just a broken contract.

label: RITUAL HUMILIATION
vc: A solitary stickman standing on an elevated scaffold in harsh spotlights while thousands of shadowy spectator silhouettes point accusing fingers from below
vo: It was public ritual humiliation.

label: THE TUESDAY BETRAYAL
vc: A theatrical calendar split: On the 'MONDAY' page, two figures shake hands warmly. On the 'TUESDAY' page, a gleaming dagger is plunged into the contract table
vo: Nintendo had smiled to Sony's face, allowed Sony to announce the partnership on Monday, and then slit Sony's throat on Tuesday morning for the entire world to see.

label: NORIO OHGA
vc: Sony President Norio Ohga standing behind his massive Tokyo executive desk. His eyes blaze with incandescent rage, fists clenched, veins pulsing on his temples
vo: Back in Tokyo, the president of Sony, Norio Ohga, was in a white-hot fury.

label: BEGGING SURRENDER
vc: Elderly Sony board members in identical dark suits bowing deeply before Ohga around the conference table, pleading with outstretched hands to cancel the project
vo: Sony’s conservative board of directors begged Ohga to swallow the humiliation, bury the project, and retreat from video games forever.

label: BENEATH SONY DIGNITY
vc: A prestigious Sony Trinitron color television and a classic metal Walkman sitting on a pedestal, looking down disdainfully at a cheap plastic children's toy robot on the floor
vo: They insisted that video games were cheap, childish toys beneath the dignity of a global brand that manufactured Trinitron televisions and Walkmans.

label: KEN KUTARAGI
vc: Ken Kutaragi stepping firmly forward from the back of the boardroom. He wears round wireframe glasses and a sharp dark suit, his chin raised in fearless defiance
vo: Then, a defiant thirty-eight-year-old engineer named Ken Kutaragi stepped forward.

label: SECRET HARDWARE
vc: A laboratory workbench covered in custom silicon circuit boards, soldering irons, microchips, and oscilloscope screens glowing with digital waveforms
vo: Kutaragi had spent years secretly developing the hardware.

label: REFUSED TO RETREAT

vo: He refused to walk away.

label: THE CHALLENGE
vc: Intense cinematic two-shot: Ken Kutaragi leaning across the conference table, locking eyes with President Norio Ohga in an electric standoff of wills
vo: Looking Sony’s legendary president directly in the eye, Kutaragi uttered a challenge that would alter the course of modern entertainment:

label: OHGA SLAMS TABLE
vc: Norio Ohga's clenched fist slamming violently onto the polished mahogany table, sending shockwaves through the wood as delicate ceramic teacups rattle and spill green tea
vo: Norio Ohga slammed his fist down onto the boardroom table with such violent force that teacups rattled across the wood.

vc: Norio Ohga standing full height, pointing a commanding finger straight ahead like an orchestra conductor commanding a fortissimo, roaring his executive decree

label: SONY PLAYSTATION
vc: The iconic original colorful PlayStation logo—the standing red 'P' with horizontal shadow stripes of yellow, teal, and blue forming the 'S'—stamped on pristine off-white paper
vo: This is the true, untold history of Sony PlayStation.

label: THE 3D REBEL
vc: Ken Kutaragi holding a glowing 3D geometric polygon cube in his open palm, casting dynamic geometric light across his face as corporate silhouettes grumble behind him
vo: It is the story of a lone rebel engineer who defied his own company’s executives to launch a 3D digital revolution.

label: THE THREE-WORD SPEECH
vc: Steve Race standing at an E3 podium with a single microphone, holding up two fingers with a smirk, while a giant Sega billboard in the background begins to crumble
vo: It is the story of a legendary three-word speech at E3 that destroyed Sega in three seconds.

label: DVD CONQUEST & HUBRIS
vc: A split visual metaphor: A sleek black PlayStation 2 console acting as a golden gateway into modern homes, while above it towers a massive, unstable tower of silicon chips teetering on a cliff
vo: It is the story of how an affordable DVD player conquered the living rooms of planet Earth, only to be brought to the brink of bankruptcy by its creator's runaway hubris.

label: THE $300B TITAN
vc: A colossal golden colossus representing PlayStation standing triumphantly atop a foundation of five generations of hardware, lifting the entire Sony Corporation on its shoulders into the sunlight
vo: And it is the saga of how a humiliated electronics company transformed a burning desire for revenge into a three-hundred-billion-dollar entertainment titan that saved Sony from financial extinction.

label: TOKYO 1988
vc: A cozy, modest suburban Tokyo living room in 1988. Warm tatami mat floor, paper shoji sliding screen in background, low wooden table, and gentle evening lamplight
vo: The story of PlayStation begins not in a corporate boardroom, but in a quiet suburban living room in Tokyo in 1988.

label: KEN KUTARAGI (1988)
vc: Young Ken Kutaragi in his late thirties, wearing round spectacles, a crisp white short-sleeve shirt with dark tie and lab badge, intensely examining an electronic circuit board with a magnifying loupe
vo: Ken Kutaragi was a brilliant young digital engineer at Sony's information research labs.

label: THE FAMICOM CONSOLE
vc: Kutaragi standing behind a low couch watching his young stickman daughter sitting on a floor cushion holding the red-and-white Nintendo Famicom controller, engrossed in a game
vo: One evening, Kutaragi was watching his young daughter play on her Nintendo Famicom console.

label: DISGUSTED BY SOUND
vc: A close-up of the small CRT television speaker grille emitting harsh, jagged, angular soundwaves drawn in sharp red ink, with Kutaragi wincing in irritation
vo: As he watched the flat cartoon characters jump across the screen, Kutaragi was disgusted by the sound.

label: ROBOTIC AUDIO
vc: A stylized metal robot bird screeching out crude, pixelated 8-bit square waves and tinny bleeps from a rusted horn
vo: The audio was harsh, tinny, and robotic.

label: SUPERIOR SOUND
vc: A magnificent glowing classical violin and grand piano dissolving into flowing, harmonious golden digital soundwaves
vo: Kutaragi knew that digital sound could be vastly superior.

label: SECRET RENDEZVOUS
vc: Ken Kutaragi meeting secretly with a Nintendo engineer in a quiet Kyoto coffee shop corner, sliding a folder containing chip blueprints across the wooden table
vo: Without asking permission from his Sony superiors, Kutaragi secretly approached Nintendo engineers.

label: THE SPC700 OFFER
vc: A technical architectural blueprint titled 'SONY/NINTENDO 16-BIT AUDIO PROCESSOR - PROJECT SPC700' showing clean 8-channel digital audio schematics
vo: He offered to build a revolutionary sixteen-bit digital sound processing chip for Nintendo’s upcoming console, the Super Famicom.

label: HOME WORKSHOP
vc: Ken Kutaragi working alone at 3:00 AM at a small wooden desk in his home. A soldering iron in his hand emits a delicate wisp of grey smoke as he works under a solitary desk lamp
vo: Working late into the night in his home workshop, Kutaragi designed the SPC700 chip.

label: THE SPC700 CHIP
vc: A macro close-up of the black ceramic Sony SPC700 sound chip. The gold-plated pins gleam under a spotlight as eight distinct musical clefs and golden audio waves radiate outward
vo: It was a masterpiece of audio engineering, capable of producing rich, orchestral sounds from eight distinct digital channels.

label: EXECUTIVES ENRAGED
vc: A group of conservative, grey-haired Sony directors standing behind a mahogany boardroom table, furiously pointing fingers and slamming audit files on the table
vo: When senior executives at Sony discovered what Kutaragi had done, they were enraged.

label: PROFOUND CONTEMPT
vc: An executive's polished black dress shoe disdainfully nudging a colorful plastic video game cartridge into an office wastebasket
vo: Sony’s leadership viewed video games with profound contempt.

label: VULGAR FADS
vc: A gold-plated Sony Walkman and high-end broadcast television camera on marble pedestals, turning their backs on a pile of crude plastic video game toys on the floor
vo: To them, games were vulgar, ephemeral fads that had nothing to do with Sony’s elite reputation for audio-visual perfection.

label: SUMMONED BEFORE BOARD
vc: Ken Kutaragi standing alone in the center of a cavernous boardroom, flanked on both sides by long rows of grim-faced directors glaring down at him
vo: Kutaragi was summoned before the board and nearly fired on the spot for insubordination.

label: OHGA'S INTERVENTION
vc: President Norio Ohga raising a calm, commanding hand from the head of the table. His aristocratic face listens intently with an audiophile's ear to the chip's orchestral sound playback
vo: He was saved only by the intervention of Sony president Norio Ohga, a former opera singer who recognized the extraordinary genius of Kutaragi's digital audio chip.

label: DEAL APPROVED
vc: An official Sony executive approval document being stamped with Norio Ohga's personal red circular inkan (hankō) seal in crimson ink: 'APPROVED FOR SUPER FAMICOM PRODUCTION'
vo: Ohga approved the deal with Nintendo, allowing Kutaragi to keep his job.

label: THE CD-ROM PROPOSAL
vc: Ken Kutaragi leaning forward with visionary intensity in a meeting room, holding up a shiny silver CD-ROM disc between his fingers before a group of Nintendo executives
vo: Emboldened by the success of the sound chip, Kutaragi proposed a far more ambitious idea to Nintendo in 1989: let Sony build a CD-ROM drive for the Super Nintendo.

label: SILICON CARTRIDGES
vc: A classic grey plastic Super Nintendo cartridge standing upright on a wooden desk, with its exposed copper connector pins gleaming in the light
vo: At the time, video games were stored on silicon ROM cartridges.

label: MICROSCOPIC STORAGE
vc: A tiny, cramped thimble labeled '4 MEGABYTES' overflowing with a few tiny pixel sprites, surrounded by a heavy metal padlock and an expensive price tag
vo: Cartridges were fast, but they were ridiculously expensive to manufacture and had microscopic storage capacity—holding only a few megabytes of data.

label: 600 MEGABYTES ($2)
vc: A massive, boundless digital ocean labeled '650 MEGABYTES' radiating from a gleaming silver CD, with a tiny price tag reading '$1.50' floating beside it
vo: A compact disc, by contrast, could hold over six hundred megabytes of data—hundreds of times more than a cartridge—and cost less than two dollars to press.

label: DESIGNING PLAY STATION
vc: Ken Kutaragi leaning over an engineering drafting board, drawing technical schematics of the dual-slot console with a cartridge slot on top and disc drive below
vo: Nintendo agreed to collaborate, and Kutaragi began designing a hybrid console capable of playing both Super Nintendo cartridges and new Sony CD-ROM games.

vc: A metal prototype faceplate stamped in clean sans-serif typography with the two-word brand: 'SONY PLAY STATION', with a glowing green power LED
vo: The device was officially codenamed: the

label: THE FINE PRINT
vc: A magnifying glass hovering over microscopic legal contract clauses, highlighting a paragraph titled 'SECTION 5: CD-ROM LICENSING & SOFTWARE ROYALTIES' in sharp black ink
vo: Then came the fine print.

label: SONY OWNS THE GATEWAY
vc: A giant golden tollbooth gate standing on the highway to the digital future, with the Sony logo on the control booth collecting all the gold coins passing through
vo: Under the contract drafted by Kutaragi and Sony, Sony would retain complete ownership of the CD-ROM format and pocket the licensing royalties on all CD software.

label: YAMAUCHI'S FURY
vc: Hiroshi Yamauchi standing in his traditional executive office in Kyoto, his face twisted in cold fury, his tinted glasses reflecting the contract document he is gripping tightly
vo: When Nintendo’s imperious president, Hiroshi Yamauchi, finally realized that Sony would control the digital gateway to the future, he flew into a rage.

label: THE IRON FIST
vc: A massive, literal iron gauntlet hovering over a map of Japan, holding golden strings that control dozens of smaller toy companies like marionettes
vo: Yamauchi was an absolute corporate dictator who ruled the Japanese gaming market with an iron fist.

label: 80% PROFIT MARGINS
vc: A pie chart carved into stone showing an enormous 80% slice colored in Nintendo red labeled 'NINTENDO MARGIN', leaving a tiny 20% crumb for third-party developers
vo: He demanded eighty percent profit margins from software publishers and dictated manufacturing quotas.

label: INTOLERABLE LOSS
vc: Yamauchi sitting in silhouette behind a low desk, his hands clasped before his face in cold calculation, eyes shadowed behind his tinted glasses
vo: The thought of ceding control of software profits to Sony was intolerable.

label: THE SECRET MISSION
vc: Howard Lincoln and Minoru Arakawa in trench coats walking briskly through a rain-slicked European airport terminal, carrying confidential leather briefcases
vo: Yamauchi dispatched his trusted American lieutenant, Howard Lincoln, and Nintendo of America president Minoru Arakawa on a secret mission to the Netherlands.

label: THE DUTCH ALLIANCE
vc: Howard Lincoln shaking hands with a Philips executive across a sleek conference table in Eindhoven, smiling conspiratorially while a secret Chicago CES countdown calendar rests beside them
vo: In complete secrecy, Nintendo negotiated a rival partnership with Dutch electronics giant Philips, deliberately planning the public ambush at the June 1991 Chicago Consumer Electronics Show.

label: EXECUTIVES CELEBRATE
vc: Conservative Sony board members toasting with cups of green tea in a Tokyo conference room, smiling with relief that the risky video game project is dead
vo: When the betrayal occurred, Sony's conservative executives celebrated.

label: KNIFE IN THE BACK
vc: A dagger plunged into the back of a corporate briefcase, surrounded by a red chalk outline on an office floor
vo: To them, Nintendo’s knife in the back was the perfect excuse to kill the video game project forever.

label: NOT A TOY MAKER
vc: A senior Sony director at the whiteboard firmly drawing a box around 'TELEVISIONS & VCRs' while drawing a giant 'X' over a video game controller

label: NO SURRENDER
vc: A dramatic close-up of Ken Kutaragi's eyes behind his glasses: fierce, determined, burning with unyielding resolve against an off-white background
vo: Ken Kutaragi refused to surrender.

label: THE TOKYO SHOWDOWN
vc: Kutaragi standing before the entire Sony executive committee, passionately gesturing toward an architectural roadmap of future interactive entertainment
vo: In a tense corporate showdown at Sony headquarters in Tokyo, Kutaragi laid out a radical vision.

label: INTERACTIVE ART
vc: A video game controller transforming into a classical artist's paintbrush, splashing dynamic, cinematic worlds across a giant canvas
vo: He told Norio Ohga that video games were not toys; they were the future of interactive art.

label: THE STIGMA OF DEFEAT
vc: A newspaper headline fading into history: 'SONY HUMILIATED AT CES - ELECTRONICS GIANT RETREATS IN SHAME' stamped with a mocking red jester hat
vo: If Sony walked away now, they would forever be remembered as the fools who were humiliated by Nintendo on the world stage.

label: OHGA'S GAMBLE
vc: Norio Ohga pushing a single massive black chess knight forward across a corporate chessboard toward a cluster of red Nintendo pawns
vo: Ohga made an executive gamble.

label: STANDALONE CONSOLE
vc: A conceptual blueprint of a sleek grey rectangular machine with a circular CD drive lid and four iconic controller ports
vo: He decided that Sony would build a standalone video game console.

label: EXILED FROM HEADQUARTERS
vc: Ken Kutaragi and three young engineers carrying cardboard boxes of computer equipment out the grand glass doors of Sony's corporate headquarters into the rain
vo: But to protect Sony’s pristine brand image from the embarrassment of a potential flop, Ohga exiled Kutaragi and his small engineering team out of Sony’s main headquarters.

label: SONY MUSIC ENTERTAINMENT
vc: The energetic, vibrant Tokyo offices of Sony Music Entertainment. Guitars on the walls, stacks of vinyl records, CD pressing test discs, and cool youth staff
vo: They were transferred to Sony Music Entertainment—a joint venture record label run by Shigeo Maruyama.

vc: Shigeo Maruyama, the charismatic head of Sony Music, greeting Kutaragi with a welcoming grin and a warm handshake in front of a giant wall of gold records
vo: Maruyama’s team understood youth culture, rebellious musicians, and mass CD manufacturing.

label: KEPT ALIVE IN SHADOWS
vc: A dim basement laboratory inside Sony Music. Kutaragi and his engineers work under desk lamps, surrounded by music mixing boards and glowing computer monitors
vo: Under the roof of a record company, the PlayStation project was kept alive in the shadows.

label: TECHNICAL DILEMMA
vc: A fork in a digital road: One path leads to flat 2D pixel sprites; the other leads into an uncharted, treacherous mountain of 3D geometric wireframes
vo: Kutaragi now faced an impossible technical dilemma.

label: 16-BIT TO 32-BIT
vc: A visual technological scale: A chunky 16-bit processor chip on one side, outweighed by a sleek, complex 32-bit microprocessor glowing with thousands of micro-transistors
vo: By 1993, the console industry was transitioning from sixteen-bit to thirty-two-bit hardware.

label: 2D SPRITE ASSUMPTION
vc: Console designers at rival companies meticulously hand-drawing high-resolution 2D cartoon sprites on computer screens, smiling comfortably
vo: Every established player—Nintendo, Sega, and Atari—assumed that the future of thirty-two-bit gaming meant displaying prettier, smoother two-dimensional pixel sprites.

label: KUTARAGI'S CONVICTION
vc: Ken Kutaragi violently crossing out a 2D sprite design sheet with red ink, shaking his head with fierce conviction
vo: Kutaragi disagreed violently.

label: VIRTUA FIGHTER (1993)
vc: Inside a neon-lit Tokyo amusement arcade. Kutaragi standing in awe before a towering Sega arcade cabinet displaying flat-shaded 3D polygon fighters throwing punches in real time
vo: In the spring of 1993, Kutaragi visited a Tokyo video arcade and saw Sega’s ground-breaking arcade game, Virtua Fighter.

label: GEOMETRIC POLYGONS
vc: A close-up of a 3D polygon fighter model frozen mid-kick: geometric triangular and quad polygons with flat shading, showing authentic 3D spatial depth and perspective
vo: The characters were crude, blocky 3D models made of geometric polygons, but they moved through physical space with astonishing realism.

label: 2D IS A DEAD END
vc: A flat 2D paper cartoon character crumbling into ash and falling away like old parchment, revealing a living, breathing 3D wireframe world underneath
vo: Kutaragi had an epiphany: two-dimensional sprites were a dead end.

label: REAL-TIME 3D
vc: A human stickman mind glowing with an infinite universe of three-dimensional geometric cubes, spheres, and landscapes expanding into space
vo: The future of human imagination was real-time three-dimensional computer graphics.

label: THE SILICON MONSTER
vc: Kutaragi and his elite engineering team gathered around an illuminated workbench as a massive new silicon processor prototype is connected to cooling fans and test instruments
vo: Inside Sony’s engineering lab, Kutaragi began constructing an architectural monster.

vo: He designed a system powered by a custom thirty-two-bit RISC processor coupled with an ultra-fast Geometry Transformation Engine capable of rendering three hundred and sixty thousand 3D polygons per second in real time.

label: SUPERCOMPUTER IN A BOX
vc: A colossal room-sized military supercomputer with blinking tape reels magically condensing down into a compact, elegant grey plastic home console box
vo: It was a supercomputer compressed into a plastic box.

label: THE JAPAN ROADSHOW
vc: Ken Kutaragi and Terry Tokunaka carrying portable demonstration cases, walking up the steps of a major Tokyo software company on a mission of persuasion
vo: Armed with raw prototype hardware, Kutaragi and executive Terry Tokunaka took their 3D demo reels on a roadshow across Japan.

label: SUFFOCATING DEVELOPERS
vc: Stickman game developers trapped inside a narrow, locked iron cage labeled 'NINTENDO RESTRICTIONS', reaching their hands out for air
vo: They visited third-party game publishers who were suffocating under Nintendo’s tyrannical grip.

label: CARTRIDGE MONOPOLY
vc: A wall of publisher corporate logos (Namco, Konami, Capcom, EA) weighed down by heavy lead weights shaped like grey game cartridges
vo: For a decade, publishers like Namco, Konami, Capcom, and Electronic Arts had suffered under Nintendo’s cartridge monopoly.

label: 3 MONTHS & $12/UNIT
vc: A calendar showing three months crossed out in red ink, beside a receipt stamped '$12.00 PER CARTRIDGE UPFRONT - NON-REFUNDABLE'
vo: Cartridges took three months to manufacture in Japanese factories, cost publishers twelve dollars per unit upfront, and carried enormous financial risk if a game flopped.

label: ECONOMIC REVOLUTION
vc: A heavy iron ball and chain breaking apart cleanly, replaced by a pair of golden wings lifting a software disc into the sky
vo: Sony offered them an economic revolution.

label: 7 DAYS & $1.50/DISC
vc: Inside a modern, automated Sony Music disc pressing plant. Shiny silver discs spinning rapidly on clean conveyor belts, stamped in minutes under gleaming robotic arms
vo: Sony promised publishers that CD-ROM discs could be pressed in Sony Music factories in just seven days for less than two dollars a disc.

label: RESTOCKED BY FRIDAY
vc: A delivery van with the Sony logo speeding through city streets to unload fresh cardboard cartons of game discs outside an electronics store by Friday morning
vo: If a game sold out over the weekend, Sony could restock store shelves by Friday.

label: HALF THE ROYALTIES
vc: A comparison scale: Nintendo's heavy royalty fee balance tipping down under an 80% weight, while Sony's balanced scale shows developer profit margins soaring
vo: Furthermore, Sony offered lavish 3D graphics tools and royalty rates that were half of what Nintendo demanded.

label: NAMCO SIGNS RIDGE RACER
vc: Ken Kutaragi shaking hands warmly with Namco executive Masaya Nakamura in Tokyo, as a glowing screen behind them displays a 3D yellow Ridge Racer car drifting on asphalt
vo: Arcade giant Namco was the first to sign, promising an exclusive home port of its blockbuster 3D racing game, Ridge Racer.

label: DECEMBER 3, 1994
vc: A retail boxed Japanese Sony PlayStation console on launch morning: pristine grey packaging with colorful PlayStation logo and price tag reading '¥39,800'
vo: On December 3, 1994, the Sony PlayStation was officially released in Japan at a retail price of thirty-nine thousand eight hundred yen.

label: AKIHABARA LAUNCH LINES
vc: A massive, winding queue of hundreds of excited Japanese consumers wrapped around multiple city blocks in Tokyo's Akihabara district under colorful neon electronic store signs
vo: Lines wrapped around city blocks in Tokyo's Akihabara electronics district.

label: 100,000 SOLD IN 6 HOURS
vc: A Japanese retail store window with a bold red diagonal banner plastered across the PlayStation display: 'SOLD OUT - ALL 100,000 UNITS GONE'
vo: The initial shipment of one hundred thousand consoles sold out in under six hours.

label: CASTLE WALLS BREACHED
vc: A stylized medieval fortress representing Nintendo, with its towering stone gate shattered open by a battering ram shaped like the grey PlayStation console
vo: Ken Kutaragi’s rebel machine had breached the castle walls.

label: THE AMERICAN WAR AHEAD
vc: The grey PlayStation console standing on the California coastline overlooking the Pacific Ocean at sunset, with storm clouds gathering over the American continent
vo: But the true war for global supremacy was about to begin on American soil.

label: E3 1995 (LOS ANGELES)
vc: The exterior of the Los Angeles Convention Center in May 1995 under brilliant California sunshine. Massive colorful banners hang from glass facades announcing the inaugural 'E3 1995' expo
vo: In May 1995, the global video game industry gathered at the Los Angeles Convention Center for the inaugural Electronic Entertainment Expo, known as E3.

label: EXISTENTIAL STAKES
vc: A three-way gladiatorial arena with three corporate banners flying high: Sega blue, Nintendo red, and Sony grey, as digital lightning crackles between them
vo: The stakes were existential.

label: SEGA & NINTENDO GIANTS
vc: Two towering corporate titans—a blue Sega Sonic-style hedgehog giant and a red Nintendo Mario-style plumber titan—looming over the console landscape
vo: Sega had dominated the sixteen-bit era in America with the Genesis, and Nintendo was preparing its sixty-four-bit counterattack.

label: DISMISSED AS OUTSIDERS
vc: American video game executives laughing and scoffing at a Sony press kit, holding up a sleek Sony Walkman and mocking the idea of Sony making a game console
vo: Sony was widely dismissed by American gaming executives as an arrogant consumer-electronics giant with zero understanding of the video game market.

vo: Sega took the stage first on the morning of May 11.

vo: Desperate to preempt Sony’s launch, Sega of America president Tom Kalinske made a shocking announcement: the thirty-two-bit Sega Saturn was not launching in the autumn as planned.

label: IN STORES THIS MORNING
vc: A retail electronic cash register with a store sign reading 'SEGA SATURN AVAILABLE RIGHT NOW!', with a customer's hand slamming down cash
vo: In fact, it was launching in stores that very morning.

label: 30,000 UNITS ($399)
vc: A bold retail price display reading '$399.00' beside a stack of 30,000 black Sega Saturn console boxes
vo: Kalinske announced that thirty thousand Saturn consoles were already on store shelves at a retail price of three hundred and ninety-nine dollars.

label: THE AUDITORIUM GASPS
vc: Audience members in the convention hall gasping with hands over mouths, journalists turning to each other in sheer disbelief at the surprise launch
vo: The crowd gasped.

label: TACTICAL MASTERSTROKE?
vc: A Sega chess queen knocking over a grey Sony pawn on a board, with a celebratory banner fluttering above
vo: Sega believed it had executed a tactical masterstroke, blind-siding Sony before the PlayStation could even reach Western shores.

label: SONY'S TURN
vc: The E3 main auditorium stage transitioning to Sony: the massive screen behind the podium illuminates with the colorful original PlayStation logo in primary colors
vo: Shortly after noon, it was Sony’s turn.

label: STEVE RACE
vc: Steve Race walking with relaxed, swaggering confidence up the wooden steps to the stage podium, hands in suit pockets, smiling serenely
vo: The head of Sony Computer Entertainment America, a charismatic executive named Steve Race, walked calmly up the steps to the convention podium.

label: NO PREPARED SPEECH
vc: The empty wooden convention podium: no teleprompter, no papers, no binder, only a single polished gooseneck microphone waiting in the spotlight
vo: He carried no slides, no video reels, and no prepared speech.

label: RACE AT MICROPHONE
vc: Steve Race reaching out a calm hand to adjust the gooseneck microphone down toward his mouth, leaning forward with a knowing, lethal smirk
vo: Race adjusted the microphone, leaned forward, and uttered a single sentence:

vc: Steve Race turning his back to the podium and walking casually off the stage, waving a relaxed hand over his shoulder without looking back
vo: Race walked off the stage.

label: WILD APPLAUSE
vc: The entire convention auditorium on its feet: hundreds of journalists, developers, and retailers standing, cheering wildly, waving notepads in the air in pandemonium
vo: The entire auditorium erupted into deafening cheers and wild applause.

label: SEGA'S STRATEGY SHATTERED
